newsitem.title: USA: Internet tax ban knocked off US Congress calendar.
newsitem.headline: Internet tax ban knocked off US Congress calendar.

text.p: Opposition from state and local governments has sidetracked legislation to impose a moratorium on new taxes on the Internet, the bill's sponsor confirmed on Friday.

Sen. Ron Wyden, Democrat of Oregon, had scheduled a vote on the Internet Tax Freedom Act in the Senate Commerce Committee for Thursday, but that plan was put on hold indefinitely after several lawmakers raised objections.
"The bill has been put on hold," a spokesman for Wyden told Reuters. "We are going to be talking with our supporters and getting it ready and doing a bit a of fine-tuning."
The National League of Cities, the U.S. Conference of Mayors, the Council of State Governments and other groups had strongly opposed the bill.
Sen. Byron Dorgan, Democrat of North Dakota, took up the objections raised against the bill, forcing Wyden to back down.

The indefinite delay is "an important acknowledgment that the impacts of this legislation have yet to be fully examined and fairly considered in the context of crucial issues involving state and local revenue systems," Mark Schwartz, president of the National League of Cities, said Friday.
Many governments that rely on traditional sales and excise taxes to fund their operations fear that their tax base could be eroded as commercial transactions increasingly move into cyberspace.
The Wyden bill, and a companion measure introduced in the House by California Republican Rep. Chris Cox, would have imposed an indefinite moratorium on new taxes on electronic commerce.
Electronic transactions account for only a tiny portion of sales of goods and services, but they are expected to balloon into hundreds of billions of dollars over the next 10 years.
The bill would not have affected normal business income taxes, "fairly apportioned" business license taxes and sales taxes that also apply to interstate mail order and telephone orders.
The Clinton administration, which last year urged that no special taxes be imposed on the Internet, has said it backed the "goals and underlying objectives" of the Wyden proposal.
But in a meeting with state and local officials several weeks ago, vice president Al Gore said the administration had not made a final decision on whether to fully endorse the bill.
